title: Bitter Springs Anomaly
summary: The Bitter Springs Anomaly was a long-lived negative swing in the carbon-isotope ratio of seawater carbonates in the Tonian Period, dated to about 810–800 million years ago. Its best-known record is in the Amadeus Basin of central Australia, and it has also been found in Svalbard. It overlaps several signs of rising ocean and atmosphere oxygen.

uncertainty.note: Sources give 810–800 Ma (Geochemical Perspectives Letters) and ca. 811 Ma (Science Advances paper, as a date for the excursion). Years are Ma counted back from the present with no 1950 offset.

where.modern_name: Amadeus Basin, central Australia (pin is the NT Place Names Register point for a spring named Bitter Springs in Hart locality, a proxy; not confirmed as the formation's namesake)
where.historical_name: Tonian-age Amadeus Basin sea, interior of a Neoproterozoic continent; no polities exist at this date

importance.justification: A widely used global chemostratigraphic marker of the Tonian, linked in the literature to ocean oxygenation.
